assessment.name: Year 10 Business Autumn assessment (Pearson Edexcel GCSE Business 1BS0)
assessment.sections: Friday 4 December, 50 minutes. Theme 1 style questions: multiple choice, define, outline, explain, analyse, justify and evaluate, some based on a case study.
assessment.weighting: Theme 1 topics 1.1 Enterprise and entrepreneurship and 1.2 Spotting a business opportunity.

mock.note: 25 questions on topics 1.1 and 1.2. Then answer one 6 mark and one 9 mark question from the Written practice tab.

cards.title: Why new business ideas come about
cards.question: Why do new business ideas come about?
points: Changes in technology create new products and ways of working, such as apps, online shops and contactless payment.
Changes in what consumers want, such as more demand for healthy food, vegan products or eco friendly goods.
Products and services become obsolete (out of date), such as DVDs being replaced by streaming.
This makes business dynamic: markets keep changing, so businesses must keep adapting.
cards.watch_out: Obsolete means no longer wanted or used because something better has replaced it. It does not mean broken.
cards.grade9: Link a change to a business decision: falling DVD sales pushed rental firms to switch to streaming or close.

cards.title: How new business ideas come about
cards.question: In what two ways do new business ideas come about?
points: Original ideas: a completely new product or service that has not existed before.
Adapting existing products, services or ideas: improving, changing or combining what is already there.
Most new businesses adapt existing ideas, for example a new flavour, a better design or a cheaper version.
Original ideas carry more risk because there is no proof of demand, but can give a big competitive advantage.
cards.watch_out: Adapting an idea is not copying it. It means adding something new, such as convenience or a better design.
cards.grade9: Explain the trade off: original ideas can earn higher rewards, but adapted ideas have lower risk because demand is already proven.

cards.title: Risk
cards.question: What are the risks of starting a business?
points: Business failure: many new businesses fail in their first few years.
Financial loss: the entrepreneur may lose the money they invested, including savings.
Lack of security: there is no guaranteed income, unlike a regular paid job.
Entrepreneurs reduce risk with market research, a business plan and starting small.
cards.watch_out: Risk is the chance of something going wrong, not the bad event itself. Say it could happen.
cards.hook: Risks are FFL: Failure, Financial loss, Lack of security.
cards.grade9: Explain why unlimited liability (for a sole trader) makes financial risk worse: personal possessions could be lost.

cards.title: Reward
cards.question: What are the rewards of starting a business?
points: Business success: building something that grows and lasts.
Profit: the money left after all costs are paid, which the owner can keep or reinvest.
Independence: being your own boss and making your own decisions.
Entrepreneurs weigh up risk against reward before starting.
cards.watch_out: Profit is not the same as revenue. Revenue is all the money from sales; profit is what is left after costs.
cards.hook: Rewards are SPI: Success, Profit, Independence.
cards.grade9: Note that rewards are not only financial; independence and satisfaction motivate many entrepreneurs.

cards.title: The purpose of business activity
cards.question: What is the purpose of business activity?
points: To produce goods (physical products) or services (things done for customers).
To meet customer needs.
To add value to products so customers will pay more than the cost of the inputs.
Businesses may also aim to make a profit, survive, grow or help society (social enterprises).
cards.watch_out: Goods are physical items you can touch; services are actions, such as a haircut or a delivery.
cards.grade9: Link purpose to a context: a café produces goods and a service, and adds value through its atmosphere.

cards.title: Adding value
cards.question: How can businesses add value?
points: Added value is the difference between the price a customer pays and the cost of the bought in materials.
Convenience: making it easier for customers, such as home delivery or long opening hours.
Branding: a well known brand can charge more because customers trust it.
Quality and design: better materials, features or appearance.
Unique selling point (USP): something that makes the product different from competitors.
cards.watch_out: Adding value is not the same as raising the price. The customer must be willing to pay more because the product is better.
cards.hook: Added value ways: Convenience, Branding, Quality, Design, USP. Can Busy Queens Design USPs?
cards.grade9: Show how adding value raises profit: higher price, same material cost, so a bigger margin.

cards.title: The role of entrepreneurship
cards.question: What does an entrepreneur do?
points: An entrepreneur is someone who sets up a business and takes on the risk.
Organises resources: land, labour, capital and enterprise.
Makes business decisions, such as what to sell, where and at what price.
Takes risks in the hope of reward.
Characteristics: hard working, determined, creative, willing to take risks.
cards.watch_out: Do not just describe personality. The specification focuses on what entrepreneurs do: organise, decide and take risks.
cards.grade9: Use a real entrepreneur as an example, but focus on the role, not the life story.

cards.title: Customer needs
cards.question: What do customers need, and why is it important to understand them?
points: Price: customers want value for money.
Quality: products that work well and last.
Choice: a range of options.
Convenience: easy to buy and use, at the right place and time.
Understanding customers generates sales and helps the business survive.
cards.watch_out: Needs differ between customers. A student and a business traveller value different things.
cards.grade9: Explain the chain: meet needs, so more sales, so more revenue, so survival and growth.

cards.title: The purpose of market research
cards.question: Why do businesses carry out market research?
points: To identify and understand customer needs.
To identify gaps in the market where needs are not being met.
To reduce risk by testing whether people will buy.
To inform business decisions, such as price, product and location.
cards.watch_out: Market research reduces risk; it cannot remove it completely.
cards.grade9: Weigh cost against benefit: small firms have limited budgets, so cheap research such as social media polls may be best.

cards.title: Primary and secondary research
cards.question: What is the difference between primary and secondary market research?
points: Primary research is new data collected first hand: surveys, questionnaires, focus groups, observation.
Primary is specific and up to date, but costs time and money.
Secondary research uses data that already exists: the internet, market reports, government publications, newspapers.
Secondary is cheap and quick, but may be out of date or not exactly relevant.
cards.watch_out: A survey you write and carry out yourself is primary, even if it is online.
cards.hook: Primary = first time. Secondary = second hand.
cards.grade9: Recommend a mix: secondary first for an overview, then primary to answer specific questions.

cards.title: Qualitative and quantitative data, social media and reliability
cards.question: What types of data do businesses collect, and how reliable is it?
points: Quantitative data is numbers and statistics, such as 60% would buy. Easy to analyse.
Qualitative data is opinions and reasons, such as why people like a product. Gives depth.
Social media allows cheap, fast research through polls, comments and analytics.
Reliability depends on sample size, whether the sample represents the target market, bias in questions, and how up to date the data is.
cards.watch_out: A small sample of friends is not reliable because it may not represent the target market.
cards.hook: QuaNtitative = Numbers. QuaLitative = Language and opinions.
cards.grade9: Explain the risk of social media research: people who comment may not represent all customers.

cards.title: Market segmentation
cards.question: What is market segmentation and how is it used?
points: Segmentation means dividing a market into groups of customers with similar characteristics.
Ways to segment: location, demographics (such as gender or ethnicity), lifestyle, income, age.
It helps businesses target products and marketing at the right customers.
Benefits: higher sales, less wasted marketing spend, products that better meet needs.
cards.watch_out: Segmenting does not mean ignoring other customers. It means focusing effort where it works best.
cards.hook: LDLIA: Location, Demographics, Lifestyle, Income, Age.
cards.grade9: Apply segmentation to the case study: a gym might target young professionals by income, location and lifestyle.

cards.title: Market mapping
cards.question: What is a market map and how does it help a business?
points: A market map is a diagram with two axes, such as price (high to low) and quality (high to low).
Competitors are plotted on the map.
It shows gaps in the market where there are few or no competitors.
It also shows where competition is strongest.
cards.watch_out: A gap on the map is not automatically a good opportunity. There may be no customers there.
cards.grade9: Always say that research should check there is demand before filling a gap.

cards.title: The competitive environment
cards.question: How do businesses assess competitors, and how does competition affect decisions?
points: Competitors' strengths and weaknesses can be judged on price, quality, location, product range and customer service.
Strong competition may force a business to lower prices, improve quality or find a USP.
Competition affects decisions on where to locate, what to sell and how to promote it.
Competition benefits customers through lower prices, more choice and better quality.
cards.watch_out: Competition is not always bad for a business. It can push it to improve and innovate.
cards.hook: Judge rivals on PQLRS: Price, Quality, Location, Range, Service.
cards.grade9: Explain why a small business might avoid competing on price with a large firm and compete on service instead.

cards.title: Short answer questions
cards.question: How do you answer define, outline and explain questions?
points: Define (1 mark): a precise meaning of the term.
Outline (2 marks): one point plus one development, linked to the context if one is given.
Explain (3 marks): one point plus two linked developments (so, therefore, which means that).
Use the business name and details from the case study where the question asks.
cards.watch_out: Listing three separate points in an explain question does not get 3 marks. Develop one point in a chain.
cards.grade9: Use connectives to build a chain of reasoning; each link earns a mark.

cards.title: Analyse, justify and evaluate questions
cards.question: How do you answer the 6, 9 and 12 mark questions?
points: Analyse (6 marks): two developed points with chains of reasoning, both applied to the business.
Justify (9 marks): choose one of two options, explain advantages and drawbacks of both, and justify your choice.
Evaluate (12 marks): arguments for and against, then a conclusion that says it depends on what.
Application: use facts from the case study in every paragraph.
cards.watch_out: A 9 mark question needs a clear decision. Sitting on the fence loses the judgement marks.
cards.grade9: In conclusions, name the most important factor and say what it depends on, such as the size of the budget.

cards.title: Key definitions
cards.question: Can you define each key term in one sentence?
points: Entrepreneur: someone who organises resources, makes decisions and takes risks to set up a business.
Added value: the difference between the selling price and the cost of bought in materials.
USP: a feature that makes a product different from its competitors.
Market research: gathering information about customers and competitors to help make decisions.
Market segmentation: dividing a market into groups of customers with similar characteristics.
cards.watch_out: Learn definitions word for word; 1 mark define questions need precision.
cards.hook: One term, one sentence, one example.

written.q: Explain one way a business can add value to its products.
model: Branding, for example a well known name (1)
Customers trust the brand so they are willing to pay a higher price (1)
This increases the difference between price and the cost of materials, so added value rises (1)

written.q: Sana is opening a vegan bakery in her town. Analyse the risks and rewards for Sana of starting her own business.
model: Risk: financial loss, as she may lose her savings if the bakery fails (1)
Development: many new businesses fail, especially if demand for vegan food is low locally (1)
Risk: lack of security, as she has no guaranteed income (1)
Reward: profit, which she keeps as the owner (1)
Reward: independence, making her own decisions about products (1)
Application to the vegan bakery context throughout (1)

written.q: Sana wants to carry out market research before opening. Option 1: a survey of 200 local people. Option 2: use secondary research such as market reports on vegan food. Justify which option Sana should choose.
model: Option 1 advantage: specific to her town and customers (1)
Option 1 drawback: takes time and costs money (1)
Option 2 advantage: quick and cheap, shows national trends in vegan food (1)
Option 2 drawback: may not reflect her local area, could be out of date (1)
Chains of reasoning linked to reducing risk (2)
Clear decision with justification (2)
Use of case study context (1)

written.q: Explain one benefit to a business of using market segmentation.
model: It can target marketing at a specific group, such as young adults (1)
So marketing is more effective and less money is wasted (1)
Which can increase sales and profit (1)

written.q: Outline one weakness of using social media to carry out market research.
model: The people who respond may not represent the target market (1)
So the results may be unreliable and lead to poor decisions (1)

exam_tips.timing: 50 minutes. About a minute per mark; save at least 10 minutes for the longest question.
section_a: Multiple choice and define questions test exact terms. Learn the summary definitions.
Outline means one point developed once; explain means one point developed twice.
Underline the business name and key facts in the case study.
section_b: Every longer answer must use the case study.

section_b.Use connectives: so, therefore, which means that, as a result.

section_b: In a justify question, make a clear choice and say why the other option is weaker.
grade9: Answer the command word, not everything you know about the topic.
For explain questions build two linked steps. Wider market, more orders, so higher revenue.
Know what a figure means, not just its formula. A market map shows where rivals sit, not whether customers want the gap.
Use the business in the case study in every paragraph, including the conclusion.
End evaluations with it depends on and name the deciding factor.
week: Most days, 10 to 15 minutes: press Start today (due cards, the new batch, then a short quiz).
Once a week, 15 minutes: one explain or analyse question from Written practice using a named business, linking each point with so or because, then mark it.
Once a week: a quiz on the Quiz tab that mixes older units with this week's, so earlier topics stay in.
Fix one mistake: rewrite one wrong answer or one watch out from memory, then check it against the card.

mcq.q: Which is a reason new business ideas come about?
mcq.e: Technology creates new products and ways to sell.

mcq.q: What does obsolete mean?
mcq.a: No longer wanted or used because something better exists
mcq.e: DVDs became obsolete because of streaming.

mcq.q: Adding a new flavour to an existing drink is an example of what?
mcq.e: It changes something that already exists.

mcq.q: Which is a risk of starting a business?
mcq.e: Risks: failure, financial loss, lack of security.

mcq.q: Which is a reward of starting a business?
mcq.e: Rewards: success, profit, independence.

mcq.q: What is profit?
mcq.e: Revenue is all the money from sales.

mcq.q: Which is a service rather than a good?
mcq.e: Services are actions, not physical items.

mcq.q: What is added value?
mcq.a: The difference between the selling price and the cost of bought in materials
w: The total revenue of a business
The amount of profit after tax
mcq.e: Businesses add value through branding, quality, design and convenience.

mcq.q: Which is a way of adding value through convenience?
mcq.e: Convenience makes it easier for the customer.

mcq.q: What is a USP?
mcq.a: A unique selling point that makes a product different
mcq.e: It helps a business stand out from competitors.

mcq.q: Which is a role of an entrepreneur?
mcq.e: Entrepreneurs organise, decide and take risks.

mcq.q: Why might original ideas carry more risk than adapted ideas?
mcq.a: There is no proof that customers want them
mcq.e: Demand for adapted ideas is already proven.

mcq.q: Which is a customer need?
mcq.e: Customer needs: price, quality, choice, convenience.

mcq.q: Why is understanding customer needs important?
mcq.a: It generates sales and helps the business survive
w: It means no research is needed
mcq.e: Meeting needs leads to more sales.

mcq.q: Which is a purpose of market research?
mcq.a: To identify gaps in the market
mcq.e: It also reduces risk and informs decisions.

mcq.q: Which is primary research?
mcq.e: Primary research is collected first hand.

mcq.q: Which is secondary research?
mcq.e: Secondary research already exists.

mcq.q: What is a disadvantage of primary research?
w: It is always out of date
It is collected by someone else
mcq.e: It must be carried out from scratch.

mcq.q: What is a disadvantage of secondary research?
mcq.a: It may be out of date or not relevant
w: It takes a long time to collect
mcq.e: It was collected for another purpose.

mcq.q: 72% of people surveyed said they would buy the product. What type of data is this?
mcq.e: It is numerical.

mcq.q: Which would make market research data less reliable?
w: A sample from the target market
mcq.e: A small, unrepresentative sample can be biased.

mcq.q: What is market segmentation?
mcq.a: Dividing a market into groups of customers with similar characteristics
mcq.e: It helps target customers.

mcq.q: Which is a way of segmenting a market?
mcq.e: Also location, demographics, lifestyle and age.

mcq.q: What does a market map show?
mcq.a: Where competitors are positioned and possible gaps
w: The location of shops on a street
mcq.e: Often price against quality.

mcq.q: Which is a benefit of competition for customers?
mcq.e: Businesses compete to attract customers.

mcq.q: How might a small business respond to a large competitor with lower prices?
mcq.a: Compete on customer service or a USP
mcq.e: Small firms often cannot win on price.

mcq.q: How many marks is a justify question worth?
mcq.e: You choose between two options and justify your choice.

mcq.q: What does an explain question need for 3 marks?
mcq.a: One point with two linked developments
mcq.e: Use so and therefore to build a chain.

mcq.q: What must every 6, 9 and 12 mark answer include?
mcq.e: Use facts from the business in the question.

vocab.meaning: A person who sets up a business, organises resources and takes risks
vocab.example: An entrepreneur risks their savings to start a business.

vocab.meaning: No longer used because something better exists
A new idea, method or product
vocab.example: Innovation helps a business stay ahead of its rivals.

vocab.meaning: The money a business receives from sales
vocab.example: The bakery's revenue was £500 on Saturday.

vocab.meaning: Dividing a market into groups with similar characteristics
vocab.example: Segmentation by age helps the bakery target students.

vocab.meaning: Based on opinions, feelings and reasons

vocab.example: The survey gave quantitative data about prices.

vocab.meaning: A business selling similar products to the same customers
vocab.example: Each competitor was plotted on the market map.

vocab.meaning: How trustworthy and consistent data is
vocab.example: A larger sample improves the reliability of the results.

vocab.meaning: Characteristics of a population such as age, gender and ethnicity
vocab.example: Demographics help businesses decide who to target.
